subject: FinEx private deployment: connectivity approach and trade-offs
content:
From: Irene Choi <irene.choi@redwood.com>
To: devops@finex.com
Cc: kimberly.park@redwood.com, chloe.martin@redwood.com, ben.carter@redwood.com
Date: Sat, 21 Aug 2027 14:05:00 -07:00
Subject: FinEx private deployment: connectivity approach and trade-offs

Hi Mike / FinEx DevOps,

Following up from our workshop — attaching a concise matrix and the draft deployment diagram (see attachments). We want to capture the trade-offs between the three common connectivity models for a Redwood Private deployment into your environment: VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and a site-to-site (IPsec) VPN. High-level asks below so we can recommend the default path for your pilot.

Quick asks for your team before we lock the pilot design:
- Which of the following is true for the initial pilot: we run Redwood in a customer-owned VPC (Redwood-managed worker account) or in Redwood's dedicated account with cross-account networking?
- Do you require private IP connectivity (no NAT) between your services and Redwood inference endpoints, or is NAT/port-based access acceptable?
- Any egress firewall restrictions (allowed destination IPs/ports) or mandated TLS termination points?
- Target RPS and peak bandwidth so we can size NLBs / tunnels for the pilot.

High-level summary (attached matrix expands each point):
- VPC Peering: full private IP routability, low-latency. Pros: native routing; Cons: no transitive peering (can complicate multi-account topologies), cross-region caveats, and requires both sides to share overlapping CIDR non-conflict guarantees. Not ideal if you want strict gateway + egress audit controls in your org.
- PrivateLink (Interface Endpoint): strong isolation (only specific service NLBs/ENIs exposed to your VPC), per-endpoint ACLs, no route-table changes on your side. Pros: fits a 'SaaS-like' security posture and avoids CIDR conflicts; Cons: additional hop through NLBs (slightly higher latency), requires DNS overrides or explicit endpoint IPs, has per-region endpoint requirements.
- Site-to-site VPN (IPsec): supports on-prem MPLS/legacy WANs and is admin-friendly for firewall teams. Pros: encrypted over public internet, flexible for multi-vendor stacks; Cons: higher latency/jitter, management overhead for key rotations and BGP sessions, and generally lower throughput unless you put an HA pair with larger bandwidth appliances.

Recommended starting point for pilot: PrivateLink if your primary concern is isolation and auditability; VPC peering if you need lowest latency and both sides can manage route/CIDR constraints. Use VPN only when on-prem connectivity or legacy appliances mandate it.

Next steps: please reply with the three items above and any internal ticket IDs (firewall/infra) so we can align. If agreeable, we can schedule a 30-min technical runbook session next week to lock firewall rules and endpoint IPs.

Attachments: connectivity-quickmatrix.xlsx, redwood-deploy-diagram-v1.png

Thanks,
Irene Choi
Director, Solutions Engineering
Redwood Inference
irene.choi@redwood.com

From: Mike Lang <mike.lang@finex.com>
To: Irene Choi <irene.choi@redwood.com>
Cc: Sara Holt <sara.holt@finex.com>
Date: Sun, 22 Aug 2027 09:10:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: FinEx private deployment: connectivity approach and trade-offs

Irene — thanks for the clear summary and the files. A few quick clarifying questions from our side: 

1) TLS termination: our security team prefers end-to-end TLS and would like Redwood to terminate TLS on your side (no TLS offload inside our VPC). Does PrivateLink still guarantee TLS to NLB/ENI, or do we need to terminate at the NLB?

2) Routing & DNS: for PrivateLink you mentioned DNS overrides — we typically prefer stable IPs we can add to firewall allowlists instead of relying on private DNS policies. Can you provide the IP ranges for endpoints for the pilot?

3) Cross-region behavior: we have a multi-region footprint (us-east-1 + us-west-2). If the Redwood control plane is in us-east-1 and worker nodes are deployed in us-west-2, will PrivateLink require endpoints in both regions?

4) BGP & dynamic routing: if we go site-to-site, we want BGP announced prefixes so our routing adjusts automatically. Does Redwood support BGP on VPN tunnels for dynamic failover?

5) Bandwidth: our SREs want a ballpark for 95th percentile bandwidth for a pilot with ~30 RPS inference traffic (avg 600 tokens per request). If you can give a sample throughput and recommended tunnel/NLB size that would be great.

If possible, include your internal brief for firewall rules so our team can raise the ticket. We can make time for a call Tue/Wed next week (we're PT).

—Mike
Mike Lang
Sr. Platform Engineer, FinEx
mike.lang@finex.com

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>
To: Mike Lang <mike.lang@finex.com>, Irene Choi <irene.choi@redwood.com>
Cc: chloe.martin@redwood.com, ben.carter@redwood.com
Date: Sun, 22 Aug 2027 13:30:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: FinEx private deployment: connectivity approach and trade-offs

Hi Mike — quick answers inline and a suggested pilot plan below. Attaching our security checklist for PrivateLink and peering (sec-checklist.pdf).

1) TLS termination: we always recommend end-to-end TLS. With PrivateLink you can terminate TLS on your side — the interface endpoint (ENI) will receive encrypted traffic destined for the NLB. NLB can be configured for TCP/TLS passthrough. If you prefer TLS between your services and endpoint IPs, we can provide cert fingerprints and mutual TLS guidance.

2) IPs for allowlist: PrivateLink endpoint IPs are allocated from your subnet when the endpoint is created in your VPC — that means you will see stable endpoint ENI IPs you can add to firewall rules for the duration of the resource. For the pilot we can publish the specific IPs (or CIDR) once we provision the endpoint. Note: PrivateLink requires an endpoint per region.

3) Cross-region: yes, PrivateLink endpoints are regional. If Redwood deploys workers in multiple regions we will create endpoints in each region you plan to hit. Alternatively, you can route to a single-region endpoint and we will do internal routing/failover, but that adds cross-region egress and increases latency/cost. We'll recommend local endpoints in both us-east-1 and us-west-2 for lowest latency.

4) BGP over VPN: Redwood's standard managed VPN offering supports BGP session negotiation for automatic prefix exchange and failover. For production we usually recommend an HA/IPsec pair with BGP so routes converge automatically. We'll share the BGP ASN and the prefixes we plan to advertise in the runbook.

5) Bandwidth: rough estimate for tokenized inference — 30 RPS with 600 tokens avg (roughly 10KB-15KB payload per request/response depending on response compression) -> expect sustained 2.5–4 Mbps average with spikes. For pilot we suggest provisioning an endpoint with NLB targets sized for 200 Mbps headroom and a VPN profile for 200–500 Mbps if you anticipate bursts. We'll refine after a short loadtest.

Pilot proposal (30 days):
- Phase 1 (Day 0–3): Provision PrivateLink endpoints in us-east-1 and us-west-2. Provide endpoint ENI IPs and firewall rule template.
- Phase 2 (Day 4–10): Run functional test + small-scale loadtest (we'll provide a loadtest plan).
- Phase 3 (Day 10–30): If latency is above target (<50ms one-way), evaluate whether peering for the specific VPC pair reduces latency and is acceptable to FinEx network ops.

Firewall allowlist template (sample):
- Source: <your subnet>/32 (endpoint ENI IPs provided once created)
- Destination ports: 443 (TLS) to specified endpoint IPs
- Protocol: TCP; verify MTU for large payloads if you plan IPsec

Next steps: please confirm a 30-min slot Tue 8/24 at 10:00am PT or Wed 8/25 at 11:00am PT and we'll send invite + runbook draft.

Thanks,
Kimberly Park
Principal Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

For the runbook please include: endpoint ENI IPs, expected NLB healthcheck ports, syslog destinations for connection-level logs (we'll want to ingest them), and CA fingerprints if you opt for mTLS. Also add recommended MTU for IPsec (our side terminates at a pair of Juniper SRX devices).

We'll expect the pilot endpoints to be provisioned in advance of the call so we can confirm firewall rules quickly.
